reference.source: Respiratory Medicine and Paediatric Pulmonology reference texts
clinicalPearls: A rare disorder of deficient or absent cartilage in the fourth to sixth (subsegmental) generation bronchi, with more proximal and distal airways spared
The cartilage-deficient segments balloon on inspiration and collapse on expiration, producing distal cystic bronchiectasis
Usually presents in childhood with recurrent respiratory infections, chronic productive cough, wheeze, and breathlessness
Dynamic imaging or fluoroscopy shows ballooning of the affected bronchi on inspiration and collapse on expiration, a helpful diagnostic sign
CT reveals cystic bronchiectasis in the mid airways with a characteristic distribution corresponding to the cartilage-deficient generations
The pattern of bronchiectasis distal to normal proximal airways helps distinguish it from acquired and other congenital causes
Management is supportive with airway clearance, treatment of infections, and management of bronchiectasis, as there is no specific therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Williams-Campbell syndrome is characterised by a congenital deficiency or absence of the cartilaginous support in the medium-sized subsegmental bronchi, typically the fourth to sixth generations. Lacking rigid cartilage, these airway segments lose their structural integrity and behave abnormally with respiration, distending on inspiration and collapsing on expiration. This dynamic instability impairs airflow and cough-driven clearance, leading to secretion retention, recurrent infection, and the development of characteristic distal cystic bronchiectasis. Because the proximal airways and the more peripheral airways retain normal or adequate structure, the disease has a distinctive intermediate distribution. The condition is generally considered congenital, and its precise molecular cause is not established.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT demonstrating cystic bronchiectasis in the mid-generation bronchi
Dynamic expiratory imaging or fluoroscopy showing bronchial ballooning and collapse
Sweat testing and CFTR analysis to exclude cystic fibrosis
Assessment of ciliary function and immunoglobulins to exclude other causes
Pulmonary function tests to assess airflow obstruction
redFlags: Recurrent severe pneumonia or respiratory failure from extensive bronchiectasis
Progressive decline in lung function in a young patient
Development of cor pulmonale in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of bronchiectasis and frequency of infection; with diligent airway clearance and infection control some patients do well, while extensive disease can lead to progressive respiratory impairment and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.
pitfalls: Attributing the bronchiectasis to a generic post-infective cause and missing the congenital pattern
Not recognising the characteristic mid-airway distribution distal to normal proximal bronchi
Failing to exclude cystic fibrosis, ciliary dyskinesia, and immunodeficiency
Overlooking the diagnostic value of dynamic imaging showing bronchial ballooning and collapse
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children
management: No therapy corrects the congenital bronchial cartilage deficiency, so care mirrors bronchiectasis management centred on airway clearance and infection control
Daily airway clearance with chest physiotherapy, postural drainage and mucoactive agents to overcome impaired cough-driven secretion clearance
Prompt antibiotics for infective exacerbations guided by sputum microbiology, with long-term macrolide considered for frequent exacerbations
Immunisation against influenza and pneumococcus and prompt treatment of intercurrent respiratory infection
Regular surveillance of lung function and cross-sectional imaging to detect progression of the distal cystic bronchiectasis
Pulmonary rehabilitation and, for advancing disease, supplemental oxygen or non-invasive ventilation, with lung transplantation considered in end-stage respiratory failure
Multidisciplinary respiratory follow-up, with cystic fibrosis, ciliary dysfunction and immunodeficiency excluded as mimics
